finding.claim: dropTable ignores the error returned by Authorize, so authorization is never enforced. Any caller who reaches the handler can run DROP TABLE. The table name is also concatenated into the SQL with no allowlist, so it is injectable. No middleware in this file sets or checks the user, so the handler is reachable without a dba role.
finding.source: Any HTTP client calling /admin/drop with form value t. A user with no dba role is enough. A request with no user in the context would panic on the type assertion at line 22, which only causes a per-request panic that net/http recovers.

trace.note: /admin/drop is registered with no auth middleware
The user is taken from the request context
Authorize(u, "dba") returns an error that is discarded, with no if, return or throw
The attacker-controlled t is concatenated into the DROP TABLE statement and executed

finding.guards_checked: Authorize at line 26 has its result ignored. There is no middleware wrapping the handler (http.HandleFunc is used directly). There is no allowlist or identifier validation on t. The sibling handler vacuum at lines 33-36 enforces the check correctly, which confirms the missing check in dropTable is a bug.

verdict.guard_found: Authorize(u, "dba") at api.go:26 returns an error, but the bare call discards it. No middleware wraps the handler (api.go:44). There is no allowlist or parameterization on t (api.go:27). The type assertion at api.go:22 panics when no user is in the context, and net/http recovers it.
verdict.reason: The error from Authorize at api.go:26 is discarded, so any authenticated non-dba user reaches the unvalidated `"DROP TABLE " + r.FormValue("t")` at api.go:27, unlike vacuum, which checks the error at api.go:33. One caveat: nothing in this file puts a user into the context, so as written every request panics at api.go:22. The exploit therefore needs an upstream auth layer that sets the user, which is the normal design.
